Generation Maine · Brand identity

Big house, little house, back house, barn

An identity drawn from the most Maine building there is: the connected farm. It is a picture of people changing how they live and work to stay on their own land. That is what this project is about.

01 The research

Maine has built its way through hard times before

Drive any back road in Maine and you will see them: a house, a smaller ell, a long shed and a barn, all joined in one line. Most people think they were joined so farmers could reach the barn in the snow.

They were joined to make a living.

In the 1840s and 1850s, bigger farms in the Midwest undercut New England farmers. Families answered by connecting their buildings and adding home work, like cheese and candle making, under one roof. Historian Thomas Hubka made the case in his book, whose title is the old children's rhyme: "Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn."

Source: Thomas C. Hubka, Big House, Little House, Back House, Barn: The Connected Farm Buildings of New England (University Press of New England, 1984).

It is the brief

Young people shaping their lives around economic rules. The farms are the same story, 180 years earlier, told in wood.

It is only here

Connected farms are a northern New England form, strongest in Maine. No flag, no lobster, no lighthouse, no state outline.

It bridges the audience

Rural and older readers know these buildings by heart. Young viewers get a line of buildings that keeps adding on, like a group of creators.

02 The mark

The farm line

A true elevation, not a house icon. Gable-front house with its center chimney, the ell and back house stepping down, then the gable-front barn with its big door. One window is lit: someone is home. For small sizes, the icon keeps the first addition, the house and its ell.

Icon at 128, 64, 32, 24, 16 px

The tittle on the i in "Maine" is a lit window, the same proportion as the one in the farm. Clear space equals the height of the barn door. Minimum width of the farm line is 64 px. Never add trees, fences, a sun or snow to it.

03 The element system

Everything is part of the farm

No shape here is decoration. Each one is a real part of a connected farm, and each one does a job on the page.

Four building modules

Big house, little house, back house and barn become the containers for creators, posts and pages. Four creators side by side make one farm. Twelve make three. The row always shares one ground line.

Lit windows

The accent shape. A window lights up in Marigold when something is live: a creator's first video, a new episode, the tittle in the wordmark. Unlit windows mean coming soon. The site gets a working reason to come back.

Clapboard

The texture. Evenly spaced boards with a thin shadow under each lap, tone on tone on Spruce. It replaces the swirls and halftone with something every Mainer has touched.

Elevation drawings

Thin architect's lines with labels, for explaining. The story of the brand, the parts of a series, how a creator's life fits together. It reads as a plan, which suits a project about building.

The horizon

The farm line sits on the edge between two sections, so the next section becomes the ground. It opens the website, closes the end card and signs the footer.

The chyron

Each creator appears with a two-bar lower third led by the icon: name on Birch, TOWN, MAINE on Spruce.

05 Website

A page that stands up without photos

The hero ends on the farm line. The about section tells the farm story in one drawing. The creators stand in a connected row, windows dark until their first video is out. Open brand/v7/site/index.html to scroll it.

Automated axe check on desktop and mobile: 0 violations. Colors and contrast carry over from the previous round unchanged.

06 Honest risks

What to test before we commit

Too rural?

A creator from Portland may not see a farm as theirs. The fix is the story, told once, and the modules used for every kind of life. Worth one question in a creator call.

Barns are common

Farm groups use barn icons. The four-part connected line is the ownable part, never the barn alone. Run a trademark search on the farm line.

Client check

Confirm Maine Policy Institute is comfortable telling the Hubka story. It frames adapting to competition, which fits their work, but it is their call.
